learn.intro: After the chaos of 1923, Germany recovered. Gustav Stresemann stabilised the currency, reorganised reparations with American help and won back Germany's international standing. But how strong was the recovery?

sections.title: 1. Stresemann and the economy

blocks.p: Gustav Stresemann was Chancellor for a few months in 1923 and Foreign Minister from 1923 until his death in October 1929. In 1923 he called off passive resistance in the Ruhr and introduced a new temporary currency, the Rentenmark, in November 1923; it was replaced by the Reichsmark in 1924. Hyperinflation ended.

The Dawes Plan (1924): reparations payments were lowered to 1,000 million marks a year for the first five years, rising later to 2,500 million; the USA loaned Germany 800 million gold marks; and French and Belgian troops left the Ruhr. Over the next six years Germany received more than 25 billion marks in American loans, which paid for new factories, roads, housing and public buildings.

The Young Plan (1929) reduced the total reparations bill to around $8 billion, to be paid over 59 years. Nationalists including Hitler campaigned against it and collected 4 million signatures for a referendum, but it went ahead.

evidence: 1924: Dawes Plan — US loan of 800 million gold marks.
More than 25 billion marks of US loans over six years.
1929: Young Plan — around $8 billion over 59 years.

sections.title: 2. Successes abroad

ul: Locarno Treaties (1925): Germany accepted its western borders with France and Belgium. Germany was treated as an equal again.
League of Nations (1926): Germany joined and was given a permanent seat on the Council — a sign it was a great power again.
Kellogg–Briand Pact (1928): Germany was one of over 60 countries that agreed not to use war to settle disputes.

blocks.p: These successes restored pride and showed that co-operation could win changes. Nationalists, however, attacked Stresemann for accepting Versailles' borders in the west and for not demanding more.

evidence: 1926: Germany joins the League of Nations.

sections.title: 3. How strong was the recovery?

blocks.p: Signs of strength: stable money, rising industrial output, new building, fewer political murders, and extremist parties did badly — the Nazis won only 12 seats in 1928.

Signs of weakness: the recovery depended on American loans that could be recalled at short notice; unemployment never fell much below about 1.3 million; farmers suffered from falling prices; and the middle classes who had lost their savings in 1923 did not get them back. Coalition governments still changed often.

evidence: Recovery depended on short-term US loans.

matching.title: Match the agreement to what it did

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that American money helped the recovery.
evidence.model: Under the Dawes Plan the USA loaned 800 million gold marks, and Germany received more than 25 billion marks in US loans over six years.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that extremists were weaker in 1924–29.
evidence.model: The Nazis won only 12 seats in the 1928 election.

flashcards.a: Called off passive resistance and introduced the Rentenmark (November 1923).

flashcards.q: Give two terms of the Dawes Plan.
flashcards.a: Payments lowered to 1,000 million marks a year at first; US loan of 800 million gold marks; troops left the Ruhr.

flashcards.q: What did the Young Plan do?
flashcards.a: Reduced reparations to around $8 billion over 59 years.

flashcards.q: Why did joining the League matter?
flashcards.a: Germany was accepted as a great power again with a permanent Council seat.

flashcards.q: Give two weaknesses of the recovery.
flashcards.a: Reliance on US loans; unemployment around 1.3 million; struggling farmers; middle-class savings not restored.

I can explain how the Dawes and Young Plans and US loans helped recovery.
I can explain Germany's successes abroad: Locarno, the League and Kellogg–Briand.
I can judge how strong Germany's recovery really was by 1929.
